request.user:
[2024 spring ms applied — problem 2]

Cholesterol measured before and after 6 months of a new drug on 10 patients (paired data). (1) Determine whether the drug reduced cholesterol from baseline (state $H_0, H_1$; assume normality). (2) Give a 95% CI for the final cholesterol of an 11th randomly recruited patient. (3) What design mistake was made?

response.text:
The numerical cholesterol values are not included in the prompt, so a numerical test statistic, p-value, and interval cannot be computed. Below is the complete solution in terms of the observed data.

Let

\[
X_i=\text{baseline cholesterol of patient }i,\qquad 
Y_i=\text{final cholesterol after 6 months},\qquad i=1,\dots,10.
\]

Define paired differences as

\[
D_i=X_i-Y_i,
\]

so that \(D_i>0\) means cholesterol decreased.

---

## (1) Test whether the drug reduced cholesterol

Because the data are paired, the correct test is a paired \(t\)-test on the differences \(D_i\), not an unpaired two-sample test.

Assume

\[
D_1,\dots,D_{10}\overset{iid}{\sim}N(\mu_D,\sigma_D^2).
\]

We want to test whether the mean reduction is positive.

\[
H_0:\mu_D\le 0
\]

versus

\[
H_1:\mu_D>0.
\]

Equivalently, using the boundary null,

\[
H_0:\mu_D=0,\qquad H_1:\mu_D>0.
\]

Let

\[
\bar D=\frac1{10}\sum_{i=1}^{10}D_i,
\qquad 
S_D^2=\frac1{9}\sum_{i=1}^{10}(D_i-\bar D)^2.
\]

The paired \(t\)-statistic is

\[
T=\frac{\bar D}{S_D/\sqrt{10}}.
\]

Under \(H_0\),

\[
T\sim t_9.
\]

At significance level \(\alpha=0.05\), reject \(H_0\) if

\[
T>t_{0.95,9}.
\]

Numerically,

\[
t_{0.95,9}\approx 1.833.
\]

Thus the decision rule is:

\[
\boxed{\text{Conclude the drug reduced cholesterol if }
\frac{\bar D}{S_D/\sqrt{10}}>1.833.}
\]

The one-sided p-value is

\[
p=P(t_9\ge T_{\text{obs}}).
\]

If \(p<0.05\), conclude there is statistically significant evidence that the drug reduced cholesterol from baseline.

---

## (2) 95% interval for the final cholesterol of an 11th randomly recruited patient

For an individual future patient, this should be a **prediction interval**, not a confidence interval for a mean.

Let

\[
\bar Y=\frac1{10}\sum_{i=1}^{10}Y_i,
\qquad 
S_Y^2=\frac1{9}\sum_{i=1}^{10}(Y_i-\bar Y)^2.
\]

Assuming the final cholesterols are iid normal,

\[
Y_i\sim N(\mu_Y,\sigma_Y^2),
\]

then for a future patient \(Y_{11}\),

\[
\frac{Y_{11}-\bar Y}{S_Y\sqrt{1+1/10}}\sim t_9.
\]

Therefore a 95% prediction interval for the final cholesterol of an 11th patient is

\[
\boxed{
\bar Y\pm t_{0.975,9}S_Y\sqrt{1+\frac1{10}}
}
\]

with

\[
t_{0.975,9}\approx 2.262.
\]

So the interval is

\[
\boxed{
\bar Y\pm 2.262\,S_Y\sqrt{1.1}.
}
\]

If instead the question intended a 95% confidence interval for the **mean** final cholesterol, that would be

\[
\bar Y\pm t_{0.975,9}\frac{S_Y}{\sqrt{10}},
\]

but for an individual 11th patient the correct object is the prediction interval above.

---

## (3) Design mistake

The major design mistake is that there was apparently **no randomized control group**.

This is only a before-after study on patients who all received the drug. Even if cholesterol decreased, the decrease cannot necessarily be attributed to the drug. Other explanations include:

- regression to the mean,
- diet or exercise changes,
- natural time trends,
- measurement variability,
- placebo or Hawthorne effects,
- other concurrent treatments.

A better design would be a randomized controlled trial, ideally double-blind, in which patients are randomly assigned to the new drug or to placebo/control, and the change in cholesterol is compared between groups.

\[
\boxed{\text{Design flaw: no randomized placebo/control group, so causality is not established.}}
\]
